tagline: Creek crossings and ridge roads through Ashe County’s mountain farms
intro: Big Horse Creek Byway follows water and ridges through Ashe County’s mountain farms, crossing its namesake creek repeatedly. NCDOT’s scenic-byways guide highlights rural mountain life here: wooded slopes give way to creek-bottom pastures, while higher sections overlook narrow valleys, barns and country churches. The guide lists a 17.9-mile drive taking 35 minutes, including a half-mile gravel section on Whenlin Ridge Road. Phoenix Mountain’s peaks stand east of the beginning of the route; the guide gives their elevation as 4,710 feet.

Transport changed this country’s connections to the outside. The Virginia-Carolina Railroad, built from 1914 to 1916, ran beside the byway and enabled Lansing’s mining and timber industries to flourish. The guide traces a later reversal: road improvements made goods and services in larger towns easier to reach and led to the railroad’s closure in 1977.

Driving north, begin at Warrensville and follow NC 194 to Lansing, then take South Big Horse Creek Road and Big Horse Creek Road. The route continues onto Rip Shin Road, changes from pavement to gravel as it becomes Whenlin Ridge Road, then returns to pavement on Farmers Store Road. That last road leads to the Virginia state line, where the byway ends.
notice: Mixed forests, pastures and Christmas tree farms share the hillsides.

moments.title: Lansing
moments.text: Lansing’s early twentieth-century prosperity traveled by rail. The Norfolk and Western’s daily mixed train, nicknamed the Virginia Creeper, stopped here, and local iron mines used the railroad to ship ore. In the 1930s and 1940s, a cheese factory gave farmers a local outlet instead of a trip to the county’s other cheese plant in West Jefferson. The town’s historic district includes commercial, residential and institutional buildings from the early to mid-twentieth century. The town of Lansing incorporated in 1928, and its historic district joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.

moments.title: Wilburn Waters' grave
moments.text: A bear tops the gravestone commemorating Wilburn Waters, a hunter and trapper who lived near Tuckerdale. NCDOT’s guide describes a second marker in the creek bed below, identifying Waters as a preacher and bear-hunting pioneer and stating that he killed 120 bears.

moments.title: Pond Mountain
moments.text: Pond Mountain rises west of the byway to 5,000 feet. NCDOT credits Peter Jefferson, Thomas Jefferson’s father, with naming it for the natural ponds scattered across the landscape. The mountain is now part of the game lands bearing its name, which protect wildlife habitat and water resources.

sources.label: North Carolina Department of Transportation, North Carolina Scenic Byways guidebook
